idiom_name: iterator method with yield return returning IEnumerable<T>
implementation_notes: An iterator method is a normal method whose body uses yield return; the compiler emits the state machine (an IEnumerable<T> whose enumerator resumes where it left off), so the producer stays linear code and consumers write foreach. yield break ends the sequence, foreach disposes the enumerator so finally/using blocks run, and the compiler enforces the protocol (no plain return with a value in the same method). Prefer it over a hand-written IEnumerator<T> unless the cursor must be inspectable, and remember the method body does not run until the first MoveNext. C#8 adds the asynchronous form with IAsyncEnumerable<T> and await foreach (separate variant).
pitfalls: Iterators are lazy: argument checking inside an iterator method does not run until the first MoveNext, so callers expecting an ArgumentException at call time must validate in a wrapper method (or split validation from iteration).

The generated state machine keeps everything alive across yields, including this and every local; a consumer that abandons an enumerator without disposing it skips the finally blocks and can leak the resources they release.

IEnumerable<T> may be a one-shot sequence or a re-enumerable factory: an iterator method returns a fresh enumerator per call, but wrapping an existing enumerator (or a Stream reader) in IEnumerable makes the second foreach silently empty - make the contract explicit.

variants.name: Async iterator methods (IAsyncEnumerable<T> / await foreach)
variants.idiom_name: async IAsyncEnumerable<T> with yield return, consumed by await foreach
variants.implementation_notes: C#8 lets the same yield syntax produce asynchronously: an async iterator method returns IAsyncEnumerable<T>, may await between elements, and is consumed with await foreach; ConfigureAwait and the [EnumeratorCancellation] attribute thread cancellation into the producer, and disposal (await using / IAsyncDisposable) runs the async cleanup. Use it when each element depends on awaited I/O and the consumer should apply backpressure by pulling - but keep the synchronous form when production never awaits, since async iterators add state-machine and allocation cost per element.
pitfalls: An async iterator must be cancelled cooperatively: pass a CancellationToken via WithCancellation/[EnumeratorCancellation], because leaving the await foreach loop without disposing the enumerator can leave the awaited operation running.

IAsyncEnumerable<T> is forward-only and not replayable, and consuming one instance from two concurrent await foreach loops steals elements; share via a channel or materialise when multiple consumers are needed.
